Jua Kesho

Jua nchi yako. Know your country.

An independent Kenyan channel for 18–30s: the general knowledge every Kenyan should have, politics with receipts, money, scams and the future. Sourced, fearless, non-partisan, clean. The revolution we drive is an informed Kenya.

Manifesto

Africa can't wait.

Know how your country works. Check every claim. Follow the money. Register, vote, show up for public participation, and hold every leader to their word. Peacefully, legally, loudly.

01

The idea

Look like the channels people trust, sound like the friend who is always first to know. A real photo, one plain headline, the facts, and something to do today. Jua means sun, and to know: Jua nchi yako, know your country.

  • KnowOne clear idea per post, useful the same day.
  • ProveEvery number and claim carries a source. Accuracy is what makes us fearless.
  • BelongWanakesho: every Kenyan welcome, whatever their party, tribe or county.
  • CleanGrown-up and workplace-safe. Edgy about ideas, never cruel, never dirty.

02

Logo

The mark is the sun rising over the horizon: Jua (sun) + Kesho (tomorrow), in two shapes. The wordmark is JUA KESHO in Inter Tight Black, its capitals exactly as tall as the mark. All files are outlined SVGs in assets/logo/.

  • Clear space: the height of the sun on every side.
  • Minimum width 120 px for the wordmark; below that, use the icon.
  • On red or green, use the one-colour white version (the sun would disappear). Never recolour, outline, shadow or stretch it.
  • Flag colours, never the flag itself or the coat of arms: national symbols are protected by law; their colours are free to use.

03

Colour

The colours of the Kenyan flag: black, white, red, green. They belong to every Kenyan and to no party (in Kenyan politics yellow reads as UDA and orange as ODM, so we use neither). Three families, eleven shades each, built in OKLCH so every step looks evenly spaced. Outlined swatches are the brand values. Ink does the work; red signs it and sounds the alarm; green only ever means good news. Regenerate with python palette.py.

05

Layout

One grid for everything, the way news channels do it. 72 px margins. Top bar: series tag left, context right. Then label, headline, the facts as ruled rows, and a footer rule with the logo. No shapes, stickers, mascots or handwriting: the photo and the type carry it.

  • Headline first, always plain words: a stranger knows the topic in two seconds.
  • Lists are numbered rows (01, 02, 03) between thin rules. Verdicts are flat solid labels: FALSE, CAP, SCAM.
  • If text grows, the layout shrinks the headline first, then the body, and checks it again. Nothing ever runs into the footer.

06

Photos & people

  • Photo-firstEvery feed post asks for a real photo of a Kenyan scene that is the feeling: the queue, the payslip, the stalled site. Sauti posts fill the whole frame with it. The checker flags any post without one.
  • Free and licensedReal Kenyan scenes from Wikimedia Commons (free, no key, only CC0 / public domain / CC BY), Pexels (free key) or your own shots. Credited on the image and in the caption.
  • Real people, real photosPeople we celebrate, and public office holders on the record, appear in their real photo: their permission, a press kit, or a CC0 / public-domain / CC BY Wikimedia Commons photo (checked automatically, credited).
  • Honest labelsOn civic posts a stock scene is marked “Illustrative photo”. A stranger's face never stands in for someone we name.
  • NeverEdited or mocking photos of real people, AI faces, deepfakes, logos, photos we have no right to use.

07

The week

Every series owns a day and a time. When a series owns a day, people start waiting for it.

  • Mon 07:30

    Sauti ya Mwananchi · Civic 101

    What Kenyans are already thinking, said out loud over a real photo, with the receipt and a dry line. Civic 101 rotates in.

  • Tue 12:45

    Set It Straight · Follow the Money · Hatutasahau · Decode

    Politicians' claims fact-checked, one public-money number, what the state did to Kenyans (we won't forget), the word in the news.

  • Wed 18:30

    Promise Tracker · The Chapter Six Test

    A leader's promise against the record, or a leader measured against the Constitution's integrity standard. Every side, same tests.

  • Thu 19:30

    Sauti ya Mwananchi · Scam alert · Explained simply

    The people's voice again, the scams hitting Kenyans now, and hard ideas in everyday terms.

  • Fri 17:00

    Proudly African: Put Us On · Made in Africa

    Kenyans and Africans doing it right, with names, places and sources.

  • Sat 11:00

    Kesho Kutwa

    A carousel on what's coming: bills, deadlines, election dates, tech that will change your life.

  • Sun 18:00

    Jua Asks

    A poll on the week's story. The answers pick next week's topics.

  • Daily 18:30

    The hot post

    Every morning the system reads Kenya's headlines and trends, writes one post on the day's biggest story, and sends it for approval in time for the evening.

08

Voice: we are the people

Kenyans don't react to raw knowledge. They react to their own thoughts said out loud. So we start from what people already feel, speak as them, prove it with one fact, and say the dry line everyone was thinking.

  1. The feelingWhat Kenyans already say in the matatu, on X, in the WhatsApp group: the shrinking payslip, the clinic with no drugs, the road launched three times.
  2. The receiptOne hard, sourced fact that proves the feeling right, or honestly corrects it.
  3. The sarcasmOne dry line at the system or the decision: “We're still waiting for the receipt.” Never at a person's character.
  4. What we doA legal action, or a question that makes people comment and share.

We say “we”, “sisi”, “tunalipa”, never “you should”. Headlines can be Sheng or Kiswahili when that's how people say it; the fact line stays in plain English. The words that hit hardest go on the red marker, one per headline.

Say it like this

“Fake job offers on WhatsApp: real jobs never ask you to pay to start.” Plain topic words, a fact, something to do.

Never like this

“People from [place] are the ones who steal.” No blaming groups, no talking down, no vague teaser headlines.

  • AttractFirst words and the photo open a question, a surprise or instant recognition. Specific beats general.
  • SustainEach line pays off the last and opens the next. The most surprising fact goes second.
  • RewardSomething to use, say or send within the hour. That's why they come back.
  • Deadpan“Only Sh304bn idle. Minor.” Lands because the number is real and sourced.
  • HypeGo loud for African wins, with names, places and years.
  • Punch upSystems, tactics, decisions of the powerful. Never down at victims, ordinary people or groups.

Post like Kenyans post

We are informed ordinary Kenyans, not a media house. Short lines, English, Kiswahili and Sheng mixed the way people text (“Hii nchi bana.” “Kwani tunalipa ushuru ya nini?”), dry KOT sarcasm (“Very normal country.”), receipts with the page and the link, one Kenyan-trend hashtag, and a question that gets people commenting. Tribeless, partyless: “nothing for us without us”. Never corporate (“stay tuned”, “we're excited”): the checker blocks it.

Sound human

Kenyans scroll past anything that smells of AI. Short lines, Sheng where natural, one strong opinion, uneven rhythm. No em dashes, no “it's not just X, it's Y”, no “delve”, “navigate”, “unlock” or “pivotal”: the checker blocks them. Real photos only, never AI images.

09

Speaking up

We are Africans; Africa's story is ours to tell. For every critical post we publish at least two that celebrate or teach.

  • Promise TrackerA leader's own words, quoted with where and when, against the official record. Kept, partly, stalled or broken: every side judged the same way.
  • Set It StraightA falsehood, a politician's claim or a put-down of Kenya and Africa: quote it exactly, say who said it and where, stamp the verdict, then the facts with 2–3 sourced proofs.
  • Follow the MoneyOne public number from the Auditor-General, the Controller of Budget or reputable media, and how to check it yourself.
  • See Through ItBought trends, paid crowds, exploited faith: we show the tactic so people can spot it. Faith itself is never attacked.
  • Proudly AfricanArtists, startups, inventions, athletes, farmers. Pride, never propaganda: real wins are convincing enough.
  • The revolution is informedRegister, vote, attend public participation, read the report, ask your MP, share the facts. Peaceful and legal, always: the checker blocks calls to violence and harassment.
  • NeverTribe, in any direction. Private individuals. Insults. Telling anyone who to vote for. Anything we can't prove.

10

Public office holders

Kenyans have the right to criticise the people they pay. We do it without fear and without error: the facts do the punching.

Fair game

Decisions, spending, promises vs delivery, public statements, votes, attendance, audit findings, court rulings. Named, with their official or licensed photo and their office, every fact sourced. Every side held to the same standard.

Never

Family, health, looks, tribe, faith, private life. Calling anyone a thief or corrupt ourselves: we say what the record says (“the Auditor-General found”, “charged with”, “the court ruled”). Edited or mocking photos. Calls to harass anyone.

The goal for 2027

Not just a change of faces: leadership in the right hands. Kenya has rarely held leaders accountable, so we do it every week, and measure every leader and serious candidate, from every side, against the Constitution's own standard (Chapter Six, Articles 73–80: Leadership and Integrity) and their record. We never endorse; we hand voters the records. That is why our verdicts will be trusted.

Call it out

  • Leaders who take advantageMoney that vanished, projects launched and abandoned, promises broken. Named, with their own words and the record.
  • Divisive politicsQuote the exact words, name the speaker, give the clip and the date, and say plainly why it divides us. Never repeat a slur or name the community targeted.
  • No favouritesGovernment and opposition, old names and new: one standard. That is what makes us untouchable.
  • HatutasahauProtest killings, abductions, hired goons, deaths in custody: documented by KNCHR, IPOA, the courts or reputable media, date by date, with what accountability has followed. Anniversaries come up automatically.
  • Church and stateCash at the pulpit, clergy campaigning, public favours to religious bodies. We scrutinise the relationship, never faith or believers.
  • Keep the receiptsEvery published post is logged with its exact text and sources in state/evidence.jsonl: the defence file if anyone takes us to court.

Names people relate to

Kenyans already have names for their leaders, and those names stop the scroll. We use them by the rules in content/nicknames.json, which the writer reads and the checker enforces. The real name and office are always in the same post.

  • The BotanistWilliam Ruto · President of Kenya. Factual or affectionate: fine in our voice.
  • ZakayoWilliam Ruto · President of Kenya. Only as a quote of what Kenyans say, then the facts.
  • KasongoWilliam Ruto · President of Kenya. Only as a quote of what Kenyans say, then the facts.
  • Riggy GRigathi Gachagua · former Deputy President. Their own nickname: fine in our voice.
  • WantamCampaign slogan. Never in our voice; only inside a claim we check.
  • TutamCampaign slogan. Never in our voice; only inside a claim we check.

Why the care: Article 33 of the Constitution protects expression, and the High Court struck down criminal defamation in 2017. Civil defamation and the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act still punish false statements of fact, and photographers own their photos. The checker blocks name-calling and campaigning, flags allegation words, and requires a source and a licensed photo. This is guidance, not legal advice: for a high-stakes post, ask a media lawyer first. Sources: Amnesty Kenya · Okuta v Attorney General (2017) · TI-Kenya on defamation law · GGA Law on reputation

11

Motion & sound

Every post ships as a 9:16 Reel told in beats: 3–6 lines of at most 8 words, one at a time, full screen over the real photo. Hook, receipt, what it means for us, the sting, the action. Words slam in, the hardest word lands on the red marker, a bar counts down each line. No paragraphs, ever.

  • Trending soundsThe strongest reach. Tap “🎵 I'll post it” on Telegram, then add a trending Kenyan sound in the app (the platform licenses it) and mute the original audio.
  • Real tracks, licensedKenyan artists with permission, Pixabay Music, or CC BY tracks in content/music: picked automatically by mood (urgent or uplifting) and credited.
  • NeverPopular songs baked into auto-posted videos: they get muted or taken down, and strikes hurt the account.
  • FallbackWith no licensed track, an original synthesised bed: a tense pulse for civic posts, kalimba and benga for good news.

12

The quality bar

  1. The guardClean and grown-up, lengths, sources, licensed photos, no name-calling, no campaigning, no tribe, no betting.
  2. The criticA tough-editor pass scores hook, sendability, clarity, freshness, voice, craft, picture and hold. Under 7.5 is rewritten.
  3. Visual QAEvery render is measured: overflow, collisions, anything off the canvas, and every line of text checked for contrast against the real pixels behind it.
  4. Cost-freeThe writer runs free on a Gemini API key. Photos come free from Wikimedia Commons and Pexels. Claude is optional, capped at $0.50 a week.

Autopilot

The self-running engine on GitHub Actions. Your part: about 15 minutes of taps a week.

  1. Sun 17:00Plancalendar.json picks each day's series, audience lane and background.
  2. DraftThe AI writer (free Gemini key, or Claude with a weekly cap) writes the week in our voice, with a photo search for each post.
  3. GuardClean, grown-up, sourced, no name-calling, no campaigning. Failures go back for repair.
  4. CriticA tough-editor pass scores every post; weak ones are rewritten.
  5. DesignReal photo, headline fitted with the real font, then visual QA on every pixel of text.
  6. You · 15 minApproveEach design arrives on Telegram with ✅ / ❌. Nothing posts without your tap.
  7. Every 2 hPublishApproved posts go live on Instagram and Facebook at their time.

15

Keeping it alive

Those who can pay, pay, so those who can't still learn for free.

  • Paid workshops

    Jua Class

    AI and automation sessions for companies, campuses and creators. Those who can pay, pay; that keeps the feed free.

  • Labelled brand deals

    Imeletwa na

    Series with brands young Kenyans use: telcos, phones, fintech, edtech, fashion. Always labelled. Never betting, alcohol or predatory loans.

  • Digital products

    Kamusi ya Kesho

    The collected Decode dictionary, guides and templates, cheap via M-Pesa, free for schools.

  • Partners

    Commissioned series

    NGOs and innovation programmes pay for explainer series on digital topics, clearly credited.

  • Services

    Autopilot builds

    The same content engine, set up for other brands. Each build funds more free content.

First 90 days

  1. Weeks 1–2

    Claim @juakesho everywhere. Set up profiles with the kit, the WhatsApp Channel and the Telegram bot. Post the launch set.

  2. Weeks 3–6

    Autopilot on: 7 posts a week, about 15 minutes of approvals. Let the Sunday poll choose topics.

  3. Weeks 7–10

    Reels every week. Run a free pilot Jua Class for 20 small businesses and collect feedback.

  4. Weeks 11–13

    Build the sponsor deck from real reach and saves. Pitch one community radio station on a weekly segment.
